newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania to search pyramids for lost life savings.
newsitem.headline: Albania to search pyramids for lost life savings.

text.p: Albania's parliament voted on Wednesday to audit the nation's surviving high-interest investment schemes and examine defunct pyramid schemes in a bid to return at least some of the population's lost savings.

Anastas Angjeli, a member of the ruling Socialists, hailed the bill's passage as removing a last political barrier to unwinding schemes that swallowed the life savings of hundreds of thousands of Albanians.
Their collapse earlier this year triggered months of anarchy and finally led to the downfall of the right-wing government of former president Sali Berisha.
"The main change is in the appointment of administrators for companies offering high-interest rates on deposits," Angjeli said of the law, which amends earlier legislation.
Administrators will have full jurisdiction over the activities and assets of firms offering high returns to depositors but excluded from existing laws banning pyramids.
They will report to a supervisory three-member council, made up of parliamentary, presidential and government representatives. This in turn will report to the cabinet.
"This bill will not destroy these firms...but makes it possible to check their viability, list all their assets and prevent money transfers," Angjeli said.
The Socialists, supported by Albanians who lost their life savings in the pyramids' collapse, want the companies audited to find out what money they have and how much can be returned.
Socialist Prime Minister Fatos Nano campaigned in last month's elections on a pledge to do his utmost to repay savers.

Angjeli said the law was in accordance with advice from the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. It created the necessary technical conditions for work to start immediately, once the government passed a series of by-laws, he added.

"What is important is the law does not impose limitations (on which firms the government can check)," Angjeli said, adding he had been told the government had already compiled a list of about a dozen firms that would be audited.
"Then we shall see which is a pyramid and which is not and what stand shall be taken," he said.
Angjeli said a "foreign qualified...person or company with credibility" would do the auditing.

Albania's new coalition government proposed the investment scheme bill immediately after its investiture on Monday and ahead of an international donors' conference in Rome that starts on Thursday. Albania is seeking international aid to rebuild its shattered economy.
At the start of the year, the collapse of fraudulent pyramid schemes sparked street protests which degenerated into widespread anarchy.
The courts are already examining the activity of pyramid schemes "Sude", "Xhaferri", "Populli", "Grunjasi" and "Gjallica".
The government is keen to appoint a foreign company to audit the remaining high-interest savings schemes in order to lend credibility to the process and avoid accusations of bias.
It is hoping international organisations will finance the operation, possibly the World Bank.

Four investment schemes with creditors across Albania are either paying back only small sums to depositors or have frozen payments altogether. One company has admitted owing money to 80,000 creditors.
